title: The Paradox of Practice
author: Paul Kirschner
summary: Kirschner resolves an apparent contradiction between transfer-appropriate processing and contextual interference. He argues that constructive alignment is often misread as matching surface formats, when transfer-appropriate processing actually concerns matching the kind of thinking practised with the kind required later. Contextual interference, which varies formats, cues and representations, makes practice harder and weaker in the short term but strengthens retention and transfer, so it is one way to implement the first principle properly. On this reading, assessment failures are often transfer failures and teaching to the test can be good when the test is redefined as cognitive work. He adds a caveat that novices need stable contexts and worked examples before variation helps.
points: Alignment should mean matching cognitive processes, not formats, layouts or appearances.
A common example of mismatch is asking students to work collaboratively and then testing them individually.
Contextual interference removes environmental crutches so learners must retrieve, decide and reconstruct.
Teaching to the test is worthwhile when it trains the thinking the test requires, such as cue-free retrieval or varied representations.
Variation helps only once learners have schemas to abstract across, so novices need stability first.
quotes: Many of us were taught, sometimes explicitly and sometimes implicitly, that good instruction is about alignment. Lessons should align: learning goals should align with how things are taught, which should align with assessments of learning (i.e., Biggs, 1996; constructive alignment). Practice should resemble the test. If students are going to be examined in a particular way, then surely they should practise in that way too. The logic is both seductive and intuitive: alignment feels fair, efficient, and professional.

Practising recognition tasks prepares you for recognition. Practising explanation tasks prepares you for explanation. Practising generation tasks prepares you for generation. When learning and later use require different kinds of thinking than during the teaching, performance drops even when the content is familiar.
This makes retrieval easier, but also fragile. If you change the situation, the performance collapses.

Good teaching to the test doesn’t copy the test. It trains the cognitive work the test demands. Contextual interference supports this kind of alignment. By varying contexts during learning, teachers ensure that students aren’t learning where or how to answer, but what to think about and why. From a TAP perspective, contextual interference is not teaching away from the test; it’s teaching to the real test hiding behind the paper.
When learners lack basic schemas, variation overwhelms working memory. In that phase, stability isn’t the enemy of learning but a prerequisite.

This brings us back to the paradox. Practice that looks neat and aligned often undermines learning, while practice that looks messy and non-aligned often supports it. Smooth lessons can produce brittle knowledge, while struggle during practice can produce deep learning and flexible understanding.
